The perception that the consumer's classic vulnerability is insufficient to explain asymmetries produced in digital ecosystems already appears clearly in recent literature, including in the field of electronic games. The problem, therefore, is not an artificial creation of the present thesis, but has already been identified by competing formulations that seek to name the worsening of the consumer's fragility in platform environments. It is in this vein that Azevedo and Torres develop the notion of “situational digital vulnerability”, noting that it may take, among other forms, a form “by captivity”, tied to relationships that extend over time, and a “neuropsychological” one, caused mainly by the application of behavioral economics and gamification <1>Torres</1><2>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 8)</2>. The article becomes especially relevant because it brings this diagnosis to the world of games, showing that, in the very empirical object given priority here, the need for supplementary categories to explain the intensification of vulnerability is already perceived. Discussing Fortnite, the authors observe that situational digital vulnerability by captivity manifests itself “mainly through the consumer's submission to the platform, which holds the items acquired for use in the development of the game”, to which are added the multiplayer character and the formation of teams as factors that keep players in the environment <3>Torres</3><4>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 23)</4>. The merit of the reference lies precisely in showing that the problem was well perceived. The critical point, however, remains whether categories of this kind, heavily dependent on the environment and on the public affected, manage to isolate with sufficient precision the dogmatic mechanism of vulnerabilization. The worsening of vulnerability in the digital environment need not be described only through broad labels of technological setting; it can be broken down into concrete factors of asymmetry produced by the very design of the platform. This is what makes the article by Azevedo and Torres useful for the critical review of the corpus. The authors describe contemporary digital architectures as structures that are “customizable, dynamic and governed by the analysis and interpretation of data”, capable of continuously collecting data, learning from user interactions and changing the environment “at any moment” to secure better results for the supplier by exploiting the consumer's vulnerabilities <5>Torres</5><6>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 15-16)</6>. Here one faces no longer a merely generic technological scenario, but an operational arrangement that monitors, adjusts and influences conduct. This mechanical dimension appears even more clearly when the authors explain that prolonged use of the service increases the capacity to identify and target vulnerabilities, because continuous data collection allows the design to be adjusted to influence behavior, while captivity makes it hard to leave the platform and builds a kind of “situational monopoly” <7>Torres</7><8>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 11)</8>. Added to this, in the case of electronic games, are irregular rewards, sounds, colors and greater graphic immersion as factors of behavioral conditioning <9>Torres</9><10>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 21)</10>. The article thus has the merit of pointing to real mechanisms that worsen vulnerability, even though the chosen category remains firmly anchored in the broad frame of the “situational digital”. <11>↩</11>

The dogmatic operability of competing categories can also be tested by their capacity to generate concrete legal consequences, and not only by their descriptive aptitude. In this dimension, the formulation of Azevedo and Torres does not remain entirely on the sociological plane, since the authors seek to link it to specific protective responses within the consumer-law and constitutional system. This appears when they argue for the “hypervulnerability of the family unit” through equivalence with the child on the basis of art. 29 of the CDC, treating the family as a collectivity exposed to commercial practices which, although they reach minors first, spread their effects to the whole family unit and weaken the exercise of parental authority <1>Torres</1><2>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 22)</2>. The same movement can be seen when they associate the platform's practices with concrete duties to contain economic power and to protect children and adolescents fully, calling on the State, society and the family to act against the harm to healthy development produced by such dynamics <3>Torres</3><4>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 22- 23)</4>. The article, therefore, shows some normative density and a capacity to generate real protective consequences. Even so, the way these consequences are triggered reveals that the category remains highly dependent on the public affected and on the specific context of application, which reinforces its usefulness as a qualified object of critical review, but also exposes the limits of its dogmatic stability as a general explanatory category. <5>↩</5>

The practical usefulness of categories such as “electronic”, “digital” or “technological vulnerability” appears more clearly when they are used to describe real barriers produced by the compulsory digitalization of services, channels and procedures. At this point, the vocabulary makes it possible to identify concrete exclusions, above all when technology becomes an obstacle to access to justice, to communication or to the exercise of legally relevant positions <1>Maia</1><2>(Maia, 2023, p. 3)</2>. There is, therefore, some minimal normative yield: the duty of institutional adaptation, inclusion and accessibility. This connection is reinforced when the problem is linked to the so-called “platform effect”, that is, the concentration of economic growth in a few scalable digital organizations <3>Maia</3><4>(Maia, 2023, p. 2)</4>. The text no longer speaks only of individual technical ignorance, but of structural asymmetries produced by platformized markets. Even so, it is precisely in this test of operability that the limit of the category appears most clearly. The core of the formulation remains tied to technological obstacles, the digital environment and access to justice, and not to the rigorous identification of a dogmatically specific mechanism that produces asymmetry within the consumer relationship. The vocabulary works well for describing a context of exclusion and for justifying institutional accessibility responses. But for reconstructing more precisely the duty breached, the factual basis, the required evidence and the appropriate remedy in digitally mediated consumer disputes, it remains too atmospheric. <5>↩</5>

The critical review of recent literature reveals that the field is organized not only around the expression “digital vulnerability”, but also moves among neighboring formulations such as “electronic vulnerability” and “technological vulnerability”. This proliferation of terms is in itself a symptom of conceptual instability: the problem is clearly perceived, but there is still no sufficiently stable delimitation either of the category's name or of its scope. In one of these distinctions, it is argued that technological vulnerability would cover those unskilled in or excluded from the digital world, while digital vulnerability would reach subjects already present, in some way, in this setting <1>Maia</1><2>(Maia, 2023, p. 4)</2>. The critical consequence is clear: the recent competing vocabulary still has shifting and poorly consolidated boundaries. The dispersion grows when several internal dimensions of this phenomenon are proposed, such as technological, technical, informational, algorithmic and neural or psychological-behavioral vulnerabilities <3>Maia</3><4>(Maia, 2023, p. 4)</4>. The field undoubtedly shows sensitivity to the problem, but it also reveals a certain classificatory inflation. The picture becomes even more revealing when specific labels appear, such as the so-called “vulnerability by manipulation”, associated with gamification and conditioning on digital platforms, including in gig economy contexts <5>Maia</5><6>(Maia, 2023, p. 4)</6>. Here the material is valuable precisely because it shows the current state of the literature: fertile, intuitive, sensitive to new asymmetries, but semantically dispersed and oscillating among environment, technique, behavior, algorithm and exclusion from access. It is precisely this scenario that reinforces the need for the conceptual refinement undertaken by the present thesis. <7>↩</7>

The circulation of the expression “digital vulnerability” in fields other than consumption reinforces the perception that this is relevant, current and serious terminology, but semantically broad and dogmatically unstable. In the debate on access to justice, it appears in connection with a multifaceted phenomenon ranging from the lack of physical access to the internet and to adequate devices to the absence of minimal digital skills for using technologies, bearing especially hard on the elderly, people with little schooling and socially disadvantaged groups <1>Simões</1><2>(Simões, 2024, p. 79)</2>. The term is used to name a structural condition of exclusion and of difficulty in taking part in technologically mediated environments, and not a more clearly delimited legal mechanism of relational asymmetry. The same reading is reinforced when the problem is described in terms of barriers to access to justice: even with the gradual expansion of internet access, exclusions persist that are linked to poor connections and insufficient technical skills, factors that become concrete obstacles to the use of institutionally digitalized channels <3>Simões</3><4>(Simões, 2024, p. 83)</4>. In this frame, so-called digital vulnerability appears as a new obstacle to access, adding to the classic barriers already identified <5>Simões</5><6>(Simões, 2024, p. 86)</6>. The vocabulary describes a structural scenario of exclusion well, but does so at a broad, environmental and cross-cutting level, proving less precise for guiding attribution and evidence within the CDC. <7>↩</7>

The polysemy of the expression “digital vulnerability” appears even more clearly when it is presented as a new general layer of vulnerability tied to the growth of technological means and to the need for continuous adaptation to a fully digitalized social life <1>Simões</1><2>(Simões, 2024, p. 69)</2>. In this framing, the term already emerges less as a delimited dogmatic tool than as the name of a general condition produced by a sweeping sociotechnical transformation. This semantic openness widens further when digital vulnerability is described as a state of predisposition to risk in cyberspaces, fostering inequities, power asymmetries, diminished citizenship and violations of privacy and informational self-determination, and is even likened to the idea of socio-spatial vulnerability <3>Simões</3><4>(Simões, 2024, p. 79-80)</4>. Added to this is the recognition that the problem takes on various strands and often overlaps with other situations of vulnerability, intersecting with income, gender and race <5>Simões</5><6>(Simões, 2024, p. 80)</6>. The point is very useful here because it shows both the strength and the limit of the competing vocabulary: it sensitively captures a complex environment of exclusions, but tends to function as a broad category of context, less able to isolate the central legal mechanism of asymmetry that the thesis seeks to delimit. <7>↩</7>

The critique of the literature on “digital vulnerability” cannot rest on the trivial fact that many consumer relationships today unfold in technically complex contexts; that alone does not yet produce a dogmatic category. What matters, for consumer law, is whether the formulation identifies a mechanism of functional opacity capable of compromising the consumer's understanding, choice and practical self-determination to the supplier's benefit. It is precisely in this respect that the passage invoked by Wada <1>(2016)</1> offers a sounder criterion. Citing Benjamin, the text shows that, in mass-scale and technically complex operations, the legally relevant fact lies not in the technology itself, but in the supplier's exploitation of the informational asymmetry of the “lay subject”. The problem arises when, faced with consumers unversed in “complex technical, commercial, financial or tax transactions and operations”, the supplier takes advantage of the “weakness or ignorance of the consumer” to impose the opportunistic logic of “if it sticks, it sticks” <2>Wada</2><3>(Benjamin apud Wada, 2016, p. 193-194)</3>. This makes it possible to assess whether the literature on “digital vulnerability” actually isolates an operable informational failure, marked by noise, opacity and the exploitation of ignorance, or merely names, loosely, the technological scenario in which the relationship takes place. The usefulness of Ricardo Morishita Wada's thesis, at this point, lies in allowing the consumer's informational vulnerabilization to be described through concrete mechanisms rather than vague abstractions. Although the work does not establish “noise” or “functional opacity” as autonomous nominal categories, it accurately describes equivalent phenomena by showing that information can be formally provided and, at the same time, materially degraded in its function of clarification, comparison and decision. This can be seen, for example, when the structure of the offer reduces transparency and makes comparison impossible. Discussing bundles of banking products and services, Wada observes that aggregating multiple items “reduces price transparency”, hindering the comparison of offers, and that it was “very difficult for the consumer to compare the benefit packages offered by banks” <4>Wada</4><5>(Wada, 2016, p. 168)</5>. The information exists, but the way it is presented neutralizes its practical usefulness. The same logic appears when the author treats the inadequacy of the channel and the informational deficit as concrete instruments for exploiting vulnerability, noting that the “precariousness of verbal information may compromise the consumer's understanding” and is incompatible with the regime of transparency, information and balance required by the CDC <6>Wada</6><7>(Wada, 2016, p. 213-214)</7>. Seen this way, noise, functional opacity and informational inadequacy cease to be convenient metaphors and come to designate concrete ways in which defective communication compromises understanding, comparability and practical freedom of choice. <8>↩</8>

The expression “digital vulnerability” will not be adopted here because, although it is descriptively useful, it yields little dogmatically. It names the environment in which the injury occurs, but does not isolate the legally relevant mechanism of the asymmetry. In this vocabulary, “digital” works as a marker of setting, and not as an operator of attribution. That may be enough to signal that technology-mediated consumption has something specific about it, but it is not enough to guide, with precision, the passage from fact to normative consequence. The problem is not merely semantic. It is methodological. To be legally useful, a concept must cut reality so as to make the conflict tractable, stabilizing what <1>p. 585</1> matters for duty, evidence, unlawfulness and remedy. When the category describes only the environment and not the mechanism, it yields little for decidability <2>Jr.</2><3>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 81; p. 83])</3><4><5>656</5></4>.

This demand for delimitation is not terminological fussiness. Legal dogmatics works by functional simplification, not by a total description of the social world. Its task is to produce operational concepts that bring the conflict back to the measure needed to make it tractable. Categories too closely tied to the setting tend to fail precisely where the law most needs them, because they keep their descriptive breadth and lose the capacity to qualify the fact in terms of attribution and consequence. That is exactly why the expression “digital vulnerability” proves insufficient. It points to a diffuse field of risks and asymmetries, but does not make sufficiently clear which form of vulnerabilization is at stake or how that form should be translated into duties and protective responses <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 108; p. 247])</2><3><4>657</4></3>.

The difficulty becomes clearer when one looks at recent doctrinal use of the label. Depending on the context, “digital vulnerability” may designate technical and operational fragility, an information deficit, behavioral manipulation, dependence on infrastructure, algorithmic <1>p. 586</1> opacity, technological exclusion or platform-mediated economic asymmetry. The result is an aggregating but poorly disciplined concept. It manages to bring real contemporary phenomena into a single frame, linked to the consumer journey, data protection, digital advertising, <2>profiling</2> and abusive practices in an information-intensive market <3>Palmeira</3><4>(Palmeira, 2022, p. 167; p. 17)</4><5><6>658</6></5>. The problem is that, by condensing many different layers of risk, the expression no longer indicates which of them matters legally in each case. Instead of cutting the problem, it piles it up. And when the category piles up too much, the evidence scatters and the remedy swings between excessive abstraction and casuistry.

This deficit is especially acute at the level of legal technique. A concept does not serve only to describe a socially worrying situation. It must offer a normative form stable enough to say what must be proven, which duty was strained or breached and which consequence fits the case. Empirical data do not, by themselves, automatically enter the universe of law. Their relevance depends on their insertion into a normative structure that makes them intelligible and operable. There is no raw legal fact. There is fact legally filtered by a normative form capable of turning it into a criterion of practical discipline <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 2001, p. 168; p. 96)</2><3><4>659</4></3>. That is why “digital vulnerability” proves weak. The expression names a state of affairs, but does not on its own provide the bridge between that state of affairs and the normative judgment that should follow from it.

<1>p. 587</1> The same critique can be put another way. The legislator and the jurist do not act as sociologists who merely portray phenomena. They start from what is in order to determine what ought to be, attaching legally relevant consequences to the conduct provided for. A category that stays on the descriptive plane, tied to the technical climate of the problem, does not perform this function well. Broad labels tend to produce the language of a period without disciplining the reconstruction of the relevant factual basis. It is therefore not enough to recognize that the injury occurs in a digital medium. It must be converted into a normatively filtered category, capable of guiding judgments of lawfulness, duties of conduct and attributable consequences <2>Reale</2><3>(Reale, 2001, p. 32; p. 189)</3><4><5>660</5></4>.

The same insufficiency also shows clearly in other competing vocabularies. The recent proliferation of expressions such as “electronic”, “virtual”, “digital” or “technological vulnerability” already reveals the perception that there is a new problem, but also the difficulty of naming it with sufficient precision. Such formulas are useful for indicating the setting in which the difficulty emerges, especially when technology operates as an obstacle to access to justice, to understanding or to the exercise of legal positions<1><2>661</2></1>. But they remain very close to the technical frame of the problem and are less able to identify the legally <3>p. 588</3> controllable mechanism of the asymmetry <4>Maia</4><5>(Maia, 2023, p. 3-4)</5><6><7>662</7></6>. They help to say where the problem happens. They say less about how it arises in legally relevant terms.

This discussion therefore adopts the expression “semiotic vulnerability”. The category targets a mechanism, not a setting. The central point lies not in the fact that the relationship takes place in a digital medium, but in the way signs, discourses, interfaces and framings organize expectation, understanding, adherence, perception of value, perception of risk and perception of frustration. Language does not operate as ornament. It functions as an institutional technique of power. The legally relevant problem becomes the unequal administration of meaning, that is, the way the platform organizes the conditions under which the consumption experience itself becomes intelligible. It is in this key that signification can be analyzed as an instrument of social control, normalization and the production of consensus, and not merely as a neutral vehicle of information <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 18)</2><3><4>663</4></3>.

This formulation has the advantage of shifting attention from the descriptive surface to the structure that produces legal effects. The focus no longer falls on the technological environment as such, but on the socially operative production of meanings that conditions how the experience will be lived, accepted and reproduced. Languages and discourses do not merely transmit informative content. They produce normative resonances, legitimize arrangements and <1>p. 589</1> make certain modes of functioning appear unquestionable. Hence the pertinence of abandoning environmental labels in favor of categories that isolate the actual mechanism by which meaning is produced <2>Warat</2><3>(Warat, 1984, p. 15; p. 47)</3><4><5>664</5></4>.

This methodological shift can be reinforced by a limited parallel. Critical categories lose density when they are reduced to the environment, the medium or the setting in which they appear. The problem lies not in the technical medium as such, but in the social relation it mediates. When a category comes to name only the context and not the mechanism, it keeps its intuitive force and loses its operative force. The same risk arises with “digital vulnerability”. The reference to the digital tends to indicate the technological environment of the injury, but not necessarily the specific way in which the legally central asymmetry is produced. The shift to “semiotic vulnerability” seeks to avoid precisely this reduction <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, p. 27; p. 31; p. 120)</2><3><4>665</4></3>.

In the IOC regime, this terminological choice is not only more precise; it is more useful. The platform does not merely provide information. It manages the showcase, the store, events, metrics, signals of rarity, promises of equivalence, narratives of value and the very framings through which consumers perceive what they acquired. The relevant asymmetry is not merely a lack of data. It is the unequal administration of the meaning of the object consumed. In such environments, expectation, consent, perception of value and perception of frustration are modulated by <1>p. 590</1> language and by design. Semiotic vulnerability makes it possible to name exactly this plane of incidence, without lapsing into subjectivism or environmental generalities.

This choice also brings an operational gain. It reorganizes the duty to inform in a qualitative rather than quantitative key. Ensuring formal access to data is not enough. Information must be correct, clear, precise and conspicuous, without excess, dispersion or barriers that undermine its practical usefulness for the consumer's decision. When communication looks transparent while producing material opacity, the problem lies not only in omission, but in how the meaning of the relationship is organized. The requirement is no longer “more information” but information capable of guiding decision, understanding and proper use of the product or service. This is what allows the move from the environmental label to the normative reconstruction of the mechanism.

The aim is an applicable and minimally reliable discipline. Replacing “digital vulnerability” with “semiotic vulnerability” makes the passage from fact to legal consequence more controllable. The duty to inform can be reconstructed as a requirement of adequacy and usefulness for decision, and not as a mere volume of data. Advertising becomes controllable by criteria of ambiguity, relevant omission, identification and truthfulness. Transparency stops being a showcase word and comes closer to a requirement of institutional verifiability. And the architecture of supply can be qualified, where appropriate, not merely as the context of the abuse, but as the very structured form in which it is produced. The gain is not aesthetic. It is dogmatic. The category delimits the mechanism better, disciplines the evidence better and prepares the remedy better.

Replacing the expression "digital vulnerability" follows from a requirement of dogmatic operability. In legal discourse, it is not enough for a category to name, in broad terms, a technological environment marked by asymmetries and opacities; it must allow the legally relevant problem to be delimited, criteria of attribution to be stabilized and the passage to duty, unlawfulness, evidence and normative consequence to be guided. In this key, dogmatics is not organized to describe reality exhaustively, but to select, among its many aspects, what matters for the decision. As Ferraz Jr. observes, "unlike zetetic theories, dogmatic ones, concerned with the decidability of conflicts, do not take care to be logically rigorous in the use of their concepts and definitions, for to them what matters is not the relation with the phenomena of reality (describing the phenomena), but rather making a cut in reality, isolating the problems that are relevant for decision-making and diverting attention from the others" <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 81])</2>. An overly broad expression may therefore have descriptive yield and still remain legally weak if it delimits neither the specific mechanism of vulnerabilization nor the form of its normative incidence. This is where the critique of the formula "digital vulnerability" holds, since its breadth tends to name a setting without stabilizing, with sufficient sharpness, the legally central asymmetry. The problem, then, is not one of empirical truth but of dogmatic yield, since, as the author notes, "its problem is not properly a question of truth, but of decidability" <3>Jr.</3><4>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 83])</4>. <5>↩</5>

The refusal of excessively broad categories is also justified because legal dogmatics makes a conflict tractable only when it brings it back to a technically controllable plane. What enters legal reasoning is not the whole environment, but only the slice needed for its normative qualification and its decision. Ferraz Jr. stresses this closure when he states that dogmatics works by functional simplification of reality, producing "operational concepts" that make the technical handling of the problem feasible <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 108])</2>. Expressions too closely tied to the setting, though intuitively strong, may fail precisely where the law most needs them, especially in organizing the fact in terms of attribution, evidence and consequence. This is where the insufficiency of "digital vulnerability" shows. The expression points to a diffuse field of risks and asymmetries, but does not indicate precisely enough what the legally relevant mechanism is or how it should be translated into duties and protective responses. Along the same lines, Ferraz Jr. observes that concrete conflicts, even when laden with many social, economic and political dimensions, become legally tractable only when they are brought back to the measure needed for their decidability, and not addressed "in all their concrete extension, but to the extent necessary for their decidability with a minimum of social disturbance" <3>Jr.</3><4>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 247])</4>. It is this criterion that underpins, here, the preference for a more sharply delimited and controllable category. <5>↩</5>

The notion of vulnerability in the digital environment is genuinely useful descriptively because it brings together, in a single frame, contemporary risks linked to the consumer journey, data protection, digital advertising and informational opacity. In this sense, the digital market is marked by growing difficulty in ensuring transparency in marketing practices based on monitoring, profiling and message targeting, as well as by opacity in testing processes, the use of <1>dark patterns</1>, the insufficiency of consent as a legitimating basis and recurring security incidents involving personal data <2>Palmeira</2><3>(Palmeira, 2022, p. 167)</3>. The category thus clearly captures a contemporary ecosystem of risks and asymmetries. This aggregating character grows denser when hypervulnerability is tied to the consumer's simultaneous position as the target of market practices, as the raw material of the marketing system and as a product traded among its members, to which are added informational asymmetry and the spread of abusive practices founded on predicting and manipulating the consumer journey <4>Palmeira</4><5>(Palmeira, 2022, p. 17)</5>. <6>↩</6>

The refusal of the expression “digital vulnerability”, at this point, follows from an elementary methodological requirement: a legally useful concept cannot merely describe an environment, but must offer a normative form capable of converting social data into an operable criterion of attribution, evidence, duty and consequence. For Miguel Reale, empirical data do not, by themselves, automatically enter the legal universe; their relevance depends on their insertion into a normative structure that makes them intelligible and operable. The mere reference to the “digital” may therefore name a technical or historical setting, but it remains insufficient when it does not stabilize the legally relevant mechanism that explains the injury or guides the system's response. As the author states, “one cannot speak of Law, in the full sense of this word, without encompassing its essential moment of normativity, for social facts are only legal when inserted in a normative context” <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 2001, p. 168)</2>. Along the same lines, the legal norm corresponds to the “moment of integration of a class of facts according to an order of values”, and cannot be understood without simultaneous reference to these two poles, which it “dialectically integrates in itself and surpasses” <3>Reale</3><4>(Reale, 2001, p. 96)</4>. The broad label “digital vulnerability” proves dogmatically loose, since it points to a context but does not, on its own, turn social experience into a sufficiently precise legal criterion. <5>↩</5>

The critique of categories that remain on a merely descriptive plane finds direct support in Miguel Reale. For him, legal construction is not satisfied with simply observing a state of affairs, because Law does not operate as a neutral description of social reality, but as a normative elaboration capable of turning empirical data into a criterion of practical discipline. The legislator therefore does not act “in the manner of the sociologist”, merely portraying facts as they are; on the contrary, he starts from what is in order to determine what ought to be, attaching legally relevant consequences to the conduct provided for, in case the norm is observed or violated <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 2001, p. 32)</2>. It is precisely this disciplined passage from fact to norm that keeps the legal concept from dissolving into an impressionistic label or the mere language of a period. In this key, broad categories that only name contexts or environments fail when they cannot stabilize a legally relevant fact-type. Reale states explicitly that “one cannot speak of a legal fact except to the extent and insofar as it is inserted in a normative structure”, which is why “there is no raw fact in Law” <3>Reale</3><4>(Reale, 2001, p. 189)</4>. <5>↩</5>

When technology comes to be treated as an obstacle to access, to understanding or to the exercise of legal positions, the methodological risk lies in turning this finding into an overly broad category. The vocabulary of “electronic vulnerability” illustrates the point: it makes it possible to name real situations of exclusion or difficulty produced by the technological environment, but tends to work more as a description of context than as a dogmatic instrument of attribution. The focus remains on the fact that technological change can render people vulnerable and exclude them, as happens with those shut out of access to justice in settings of electronic proceedings, Online Courts, Justice 4.0, Justice 5.0 and ODR platforms <1>Maia</1><2>(Maia, 2023, p. 7)</2>. This formulation has real descriptive merit, but its explanatory force rests mainly on the idea of a technological obstacle, and not on a finer identification of the legal mechanism that turns this barrier into a controllable asymmetry within a regime such as the CDC's. The category points to the context of exclusion, but does not stabilize, with the desirable sharpness, the specific way in which the injury is produced. This becomes even clearer when the problem is placed within the broad horizon of Society 5.0, the 4th Industrial Revolution and their systemic effects on access, which call for special attention to the so-called technologically vulnerabilized <3>Maia</3><4>(Maia, 2023, p. 5)</4>. The summary of the so-called sixth renewal wave of access to justice confirms this design: it is presented as a field devoted to analyzing and mitigating technology as an obstacle to a just legal order <5>Maia</5><6>(Maia, 2023, p. 7)</6>. The vocabulary helps to name the barrier, but still falls short of explaining, with sufficient precision, the legal mechanism of the asymmetry. <7>↩</7>

The recent proliferation of labels such as “electronic”, “digital”, “virtual” or “technological vulnerability” already reveals, by itself, an important methodological difficulty: the field perceives that there is a new problem, but still wavers over how to name it. These expressions are descriptively useful for indicating that certain asymmetries emerge in a technically mediated environment, but they tend to stay very close to the setting in which the injury occurs, and are less able to identify, with dogmatic sharpness, the legally relevant mechanism of vulnerabilization. It is in this sense that one speaks of “cyber or electronic vulnerability”, also called virtual, technological or digital vulnerability, when technology comes to function as an obstacle to access to justice <1>Maia</1><2>(Maia, 2023, p. 3)</2>. This feature is reinforced when the terminological dispute itself turns on whether “digital” or “electronic” covers more ground, that is, on which name best covers the technical environment, and not on which category best individualizes the legally controllable factual basis. The remark that “electronic” could be an even broader term, since it also reaches digital phenomena, makes it all the more visible how far the axis of the formulation remains centered on the technological frame of the problem <3>Maia</3><4>(Maia, 2023, p. 3-4)</4>. The category comes to name the technical climate of the injury, but not necessarily its mechanism. The same happens when technological vulnerability is described as an individual's technical, informational, material or organizational limitation in dealing with information and communication technologies <5>Maia</5><6>(Maia, 2023, p. 4)</6>. It helps to say where the problem happens and in what kind of setting it intensifies, but still offers less precision for reconstructing, in a consumer-law key, duty, evidence, attribution and remedy. <7>↩</7>

The refusal of the expression “digital vulnerability”, at this point, can be taken further with Luis Alberto Warat, because his semiology of power shifts the focus from the mere technical environment to the mechanism that actually matters in producing subjection. The problem lies not in the “digital” taken as a generic setting, but in the way signs, discourses and communicative framings organize understanding, expectation and adherence. Warat states explicitly that signification must be analyzed “as an instrument of social control”, “as a normalizing and disciplinary strategy of individuals”, “as a formula producing consensus” and “as persuasive power provoking effects of verisimilitude over the material conditions of social life” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 18)</2>. The decisive point, therefore, is not technology as such, but the semiotic work that turns certain conditions of power into an appearance of normality, validity and inevitability. In this key, a more precise legal category must target the mechanism of unequal intelligibility and semiotic capture, and not merely the fact that the relationship takes place in a digital environment. <3>↩</3>

Warat also offers a useful basis for justifying a legal category centered on mechanism rather than setting, because his reflection on language shifts attention from the descriptive surface to the socially operative production of effects of meaning. For him, languages are not limited to the informative content they seem to transmit; they engender “significant and normalizing resonances of social practices”, taking part in a deeper dynamic of “social production of meanings” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 15)</2>. This makes it clear that the legally relevant problem lies not only in identifying the technical context in which the relationship occurs, but in grasping how signification organizes in advance the intelligibility of experience and conditions how it will be lived, accepted and reproduced. Along the same lines, Warat observes that pragmatic analysis makes it possible to articulate functions such as “persuasion, legitimation, anticipation”, showing how certain discourses produce an “effect of unquestionability and reality over knowledge” <3>Warat</3><4>(Warat, 1984, p. 47)</4>. Hence the pertinence of abandoning broad, environmental labels in favor of categories that isolate the actual mechanism by which meaning is produced. <5>↩</5>

Critical categories lose density when they are reduced to the environment, the medium or the setting in which they appear. The warning comes through clearly in the formulation according to which the spectacle is not to be confused with a set of images or with its technical means of diffusion, but consists in a social relation mediated by images <1>Debord</1><2>(Debord, 2013, p. 27)</2>. Reducing it to the mass media therefore grasps only its most visible surface manifestation, and not the structural mechanism the category seeks to describe <3>Debord</3><4>(Debord, 2013, p. 31)</4>. The same methodological reasoning makes it possible to reject formulations that, though intuitively expressive, end up naming only the setting in which the injury occurs. The risk is keeping descriptive force while losing dogmatic operability, because the category comes to point to a context without stabilizing, with sufficient sharpness, the relevant factual basis, the duty strained, the required evidentiary standard and the corresponding legal consequence. The critique of reducing the spectacle to “the media”, precisely because this turns it back into a mere instrument and erases the social logic the category sought to denounce, reinforces this methodological caution <5>Debord</5><6>(Debord, 2013, p. 120)</6>. Likewise, the expression “digital vulnerability” tends to grow poorer when it describes the technological environment without isolating the specific way in which the legally relevant asymmetry is produced. The shift to “semiotic vulnerability” therefore does not stem from a preference of vocabulary, but from the search for a category better able to identify the actual mechanism of vulnerabilization, located in the unequal administration of meaning, expectation, perception of risk, the intelligibility of the offer and the conditions for contesting it. <7>↩</7>

In consumer relations, the problem of information was never merely quantitative. Contract, offer, interface and rules are forms of language, and it is through them that the market organizes expectation, adherence, comparison and resistance. A significant part of contractual injustice therefore arises not from the plain absence of data, but from the way legally relevant meaning is produced, distributed and withheld. In a platform environment, consumers may receive texts, dialog boxes, links, policies and notices in abundance and still remain beyond any real understanding of what they accept. It is on this plane that semiotic vulnerability becomes intelligible in its communicative aspect. The law faces not merely a failure of information, but a regime of communication that determines who is able to understand, who is able to compare and who is able to contest.

The CDC already contains the normative core of this problem. The offer and presentation of products or services must ensure correct, clear, precise and conspicuous information<1><2>681</2></1>. This means that the technical complexity of supply does not entitle the supplier to hide behind indecipherable vocabulary, cascades of documents or communicative architectures that deliver words and withhold meaning. Likewise, consumer contracts do not bind consumers who are not given a real opportunity to learn their content beforehand, nor when they are drafted in a way that hinders understanding of their meaning and scope<3><4>682</4></3>. The decisive point, therefore, is not proving that “the text was there”, but assessing whether the legally relevant meaning could actually be known.

<1>p. 602</1> This conclusion requires recognizing that language is not a neutral vehicle. Normative, contractual and institutional texts operate as techniques for producing selective intelligibility. They do not merely inform; they stabilize meanings, distribute access to significance and filter the possible readings in advance. Strictly speaking, contract and interface are not transparent containers of data, but institutional forms of organizing meaning. Legal and regulatory language is always shot through with strategic, ideological and pragmatic factors, which is why the problem of consent cannot be reduced to the physical availability of the statement. Consumers may receive the text, click, accept and even repeat its terms without actually grasping what it means in practice<2><3>683</3></2>.

The point goes deeper once one sees that the coherent organization of discourse also silences problems, excludes uncomfortable readings and stabilizes a semantic frame controlled in advance. The appearance of univocity, closure and naturalness in the contractual text is not necessarily a sign of neutrality. Often it works precisely as a mechanism of communicative subjection. What is at stake is not only what the text says expressly, but how it defines the field of what can be said, compared and contested<1><2>684</2></1>. On platforms this is especially important, because contractual language <3>p. 603</3> does not come alone. It works together with the interface, the sign-up flow, the selective highlighting of information, the placement of links and visual framings that steer consumers to accept before they understand.

This is why the asymmetry does not stem only from missing information. It can be produced by special languages that function as barriers of competence. Consumers receive the text, but not real access to the code that organizes its meaning. Technical, legal and business language has a social function of distinction and exclusion. It speaks to the initiated and, at the same time, reaffirms the position of those who master the code. In practical terms, merely making terms, policies or notices available does not eliminate semiotic exclusion when full understanding remains reserved to those who master the system's grammar<1><2>685</2></1>. The difficulty, then, is not episodic. It is structural. Consumers do not merely get one piece of data wrong. They adhere within a frame of language that already places them outside the center of intelligibility of the relationship.

It is at this point that one can speak of meaning-vitiated consent. This is not a one-off factual error, such as mistaking a price or a single deadline. It is an inability, <1>p. 604</1> structurally produced by the communicative conditions of supply, to decode, compare and anticipate relevant consequences. Submission stems not only from express omission, but from an architecture of language, interface and framing that conditions in advance access to the legal and economic meaning of the decision. Consumers may be formally informed and still be materially cut off from the meaning of what they accept. This is the communicative form of semiotic vulnerability.

Under the CDC, this brings the problem back to the duty to inform in its material sense. Suppliers do not discharge this duty merely by making the content technically accessible through a click, a scroll or a download. What matters is whether the average consumer could read and understand what those clauses meant, which rights and obligations were being assumed and what practical consequences followed from adhering. A bare reference to the existence of general terms is not enough when the meaning remains opaque<1><2>686</2></1>. In this picture, the principle of transparency is no peripheral formality. It goes to the very essence of the transaction, because information forms part of the content of the contract and, if it fails, it compromises the legal quality of the performance.

This explains why contractual obscurity, in consumer relations, is not an innocent stylistic flaw. It is evidence of structural disloyalty in the way consent is organized. In adhesion contracts, consumers take no part in the drafting and enter the relationship trusting that there is a minimum of textual intelligibility and fairness. Review of these clauses is therefore not limited to a neutral grammatical examination, but is guided by objective good faith and by the protection of the adhering party's trust. Pre-drafted clauses must be read so as to respect the legitimate interests of those who accepted them without being able to negotiate them, and obscure drafting triggers precisely the presumption that the supplier failed in its duty to organize consent on fair terms<1><2>687</2></1>.

<1>p. 605</1> This asymmetric communicative regime also helps to explain why semiotic vulnerability is not a loose cultural metaphor. It describes a real disadvantage in decoding, comparing and resisting, produced by the way the market organizes its language. In IOCs, this is amplified because the supplier's communication is not limited to the written contract. It extends to showcases, in-game stores, purchase screens, event messages, update announcements, metrics, rankings, signals of rarity and framings of value that are part of the consumption experience. Consumers face not just a text. They face an entire grammar of governed enjoyment.

The dogmatic consequence is twofold. First, the duty to inform must be read as a duty of intelligibility, adequacy and verifiability, and not as the mere delivery of a volume of documents. Second, consumer protection in platform environments requires <1>standards</1> capable of reducing the asymmetry of meaning and the asymmetry of evidence at the same time. If the platform controls the language through which the object is presented, understood and accepted, it also tends to control the records, framings and traces through which adherence and frustration may later be reconstructed. Language, code and consent are therefore not a peripheral topic. They are one of the grounds that justify, in what follows, requirements of open auditability and criteria of restoration by functional value equivalence.

“Art. 31. The offer and presentation of products or services must ensure correct, clear, precise and conspicuous information, in the Portuguese language, about their characteristics, qualities, quantity, composition, price, warranty, expiry dates and origin, among other data, as well as about the risks they pose to the health and safety of consumers.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>. <3>↩</3>

Legal and institutional language is not neutral; it operates as a technique for producing and stabilizing meaning, steeped in political and strategic factors, which rules out the image of the contract or the interface as mere transparent containers of information. Pragmatics applied to law makes it possible to see that ideology is “a factor inseparable from the conceptual structure made explicit in general norms”, which requires the interpreter to read in a way that uncovers “the connections between the words of the law and the political and ideological factors that produce and determine their functions in society” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 47)</2>. Legal language thus does not merely inform; it organizes some possible intelligibilities and blocks others. This finding is crucial for understanding how consumer consent can be vitiated by structurally produced meaning, and not merely by a one-off absence of data. Normative discourses involve a “game of persuasion and mythification” that stereotypes meanings and legitimizes the reproduction of power under an appearance of normality <3>Warat</3><4>(Warat, 1984, p. 45)</4>. Through the use of “a language impregnated with stereotyped significations”, what is introduced, “under the supposed appearance of an objective description, is an ideological dimension not formulated in legal language”, the central aim of such expressions being “to influence and determine opinions” <5>Warat</5><6>(Warat, 1984, p. 71)</6>. As a result, consumers may perfectly well receive the text, click, accept and even repeat its terms without ever grasping what it really means in practice, because communicative subjection depends not only on lack of access to the statement, but on the selective and asymmetric way in which meaning is produced for them. <7>↩</7>

Normative, contractual and regulatory texts produce selective intelligibility and can organize forms of communicative subjection, since the coherent organization of discourse itself works as a filtering mechanism that silences problems and excludes uncomfortable readings. The “coherent organization of a discourse” can “silence problems” and, through these silences, perform “political functions in society”, while it “explicitly forces subjects to say or repress certain things” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 50)</2>. Intelligibility is thus not distributed neutrally; it is produced selectively. This selectivity is reinforced when legal discourse presents itself with an appearance of univocity and closure: belief in normative univocity presupposes “prior ideological coincidence”, and the unalterability of signifiers sustains the ideal of a rational norm precisely because it secures certain “social effects of the law in society” <3>Warat</3><4>(Warat, 1984, p. 68)</4>. The critique of the claim that legal language is closed shows that the demands for totality and closure of the system are not mere logical requirements, but ideological representations that serve specific functions of the legal form <5>Warat</5><6>(Warat, 1984, p. 54)</6>. As a result, institutional texts can organize communicative subjection not only through what they say expressly, but through the way they stabilize meanings, exclude interpretive alternatives and induce adherence to a semantic frame controlled in advance. Acceptance of rules, framings and institutional conditions can be produced discursively, with no need for an explicit command, through a “discursive work” that manipulates words and stereotypes to manufacture acceptance and naturalize authority. Consensus on the legitimacy of power results from discursive work, which is effective precisely because it operates through “a game of stereotyping”, whose primary function is legitimation <7>Warat</7><8>(Warat, 1984, p. 18)</8>. Power produces meanings that make adherence seem spontaneous, reasonable or inevitable, constituting an “ordered subjectivity”, shaped by the “social idiom” and progressively alienated from the ends of the power that shapes it. In this situation physical violence becomes largely dispensable, replaced by “significant violence” and “imaginary violence”, which can neutralize the critical power of subjectivity and produce internalized obedience <9>Warat</9><10>(Warat, 1984, p. 110)</10>. Certain effects of acceptance spread with no need for explicit demonstration, relying on stereotypes, topical formulas and beliefs already settled, so that discursive alignment spreads “like an infection” or “contagion” <11>Warat</11><12>(Warat, 1984, p. 88)</12>. Communicative subjection therefore depends not only on what is said in imperative form, but on the production of a horizon of meaning in which obeying, adhering or accepting comes to seem simply the normal course of things. <13>↩</13>

In platform-mediated contractual environments, the fragility of consent stems not only from the absence of information, but also from the organization of a functionally exclusionary language, which allows the message to be formally received without ensuring actual access to its meaning. The problem is therefore not reduced to the occasional lack of a given piece of data, but involves a structural asymmetry of intelligibility: consumers come into contact with text, interface and contracting commands, but remain outside the code that organizes the real legal meaning of the transaction. This is where Gnerre offers direct support, by showing that certain specialized languages serve not only to communicate, but also to distinguish and exclude. As he states, "the central function of all special languages is social: they have a real communicative value but they exclude from communication the people of the linguistic community external to the group that uses the special language and, on the other hand, they have the function of reaffirming the identity of the members of the reduced group that has access to the special language." <1>Gnerre</1><2>(Gnerre, 1991, p. 23)</2>. Merely making terms, policies or notices available therefore does not eliminate semiotic exclusion when full understanding remains reserved to those initiated in the technical, business or legal code of the relationship. Along the same lines, Gnerre observes that "language constitutes the most powerful barbed wire for blocking access to power", adding that drafting a document with legal value requires more than knowing the language in the ordinary sense, since one must master "a whole complex and archaizing phraseology that is customary" <3>Gnerre</3><4>(Gnerre, 1991, p. 22)</4>. Transposed to digital consumption, this shows that a defect of consent may arise not only from concealing information, but from the structural withholding of meaning itself. <5>↩</5>

Under the CDC, the duty to inform is not satisfied by merely making content formally available, nor by the bare physical existence of clauses accessible through a click, a scroll or a reading that is possible in the abstract. It is a material duty of clarity and understanding, aimed at ensuring that consumers have actual access to the legal and practical meaning of what is presented to them as the basis of consent. Communicative asymmetry is therefore not resolved by proof that the text was "there", but by establishing that its content could really be known by the average consumer, especially in contexts of strong unilateral pre-drafting: "the mere mention that CONDGs will be used in the contract is not enough, it is necessary that the ordinary man can read and understand what those clauses mean, which obligations and rights he is accepting" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 91-92)</2>. The exclusion of intelligibility undermines the legitimacy of consent because it affects the very material content of the information legally owed, in conflict with objective good faith and the protection of trust. The principle of transparency governs the pre-contractual stage and the conclusion of the contract itself, being "more than a mere formal element", since it "affects the essence of the transaction", as information "is part of the content of the contract or, if it fails, represents a failure in the quality of the product or service offered" <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 819)</4>. Obscure texts and communicative architectures that deliver words while withholding meaning produce a zone of materially vitiated consent. <5>↩</5>

Under the CDC system, review of adhesion contracts and obscure drafting is not limited to a neutral grammatical examination, but is guided by objective good faith and by the protection of consumer trust, in light of contractual justice and the legitimate expectations of the adhering party. With pre-drafted clauses, consumers take no part in formulating the text and often enter the relationship trusting that the drafting respects a minimum of fairness and intelligibility. The new function of contract law therefore puts the principle of interpretation in accordance with good faith back at the center, so that art. 47 of the CDC, together with the general clause of art. 51, IV, allows pre-drafted clauses to be interpreted "in a way that respects the trust and the legitimate interests of the consumers who accepted these pre-drafted clauses" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 94-95)</2>. Obscurity is not an aesthetic flaw, but evidence of structural disloyalty in the way consent is organized. Breach of the duty of clear drafting is sanctioned by art. 46 of the CDC, under which contracts do not bind consumers if they are drafted in a way that hinders understanding of their meaning and scope, a sanction rooted in the "presumption of bad faith of the supplier-drafter of the contract" <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 902-903)</4>. An incomprehensible clause is not proof of robust consent; it is a symptom of betrayed trust with a veneer of drafting. <5>↩</5>

Semiotic vulnerability acquires dogmatic usefulness only when it ceases to function as a general diagnosis of the environment and begins to operate as a scheme of attribution and control. In IOCs, this requires disciplining three distinct and interlinked planes: the mechanism alleged, the objective basis on which this mechanism can be demonstrated and the typical consequence that the CDC already allows to be drawn from it. The point is not to assert, impressionistically, that the consumer was “manipulated” or “confused”. The point is to show that the communicational regime of supply was structured so as to produce a relevant asymmetry of <1>p. 606</1> understanding, comparison and contestation, and that this asymmetry can be traced back to legally controllable duties, defects and remedies.

On the first plane, what is alleged is not a failure to read, individual distraction or psychological incapacity of the consumer. The allegation falls on a communicational and architectural structure that distributes power. In IOCs, the platform controls language, framings, signals of equivalence, criteria of rarity, acceptance flows, update messages and forms of visibility of the object itself. This means that it not only informs about enjoyment, but administers the means by which enjoyment will be perceived and evaluated. The asymmetry, therefore, does not arise from a subjective deficiency of the user, but from an unequal distribution of communicational competence and of the power to define meaning<1><2>688</2></1>. For this reason, semiotic vulnerability can be alleged as a legal fact: the supplier organizes in advance the field of what can be understood, compared and accepted.

This structure is aggravated because, in IOC ecosystems, the governance of meaning is continuous. The platform does not limit itself to communicating once, at the moment of contracting. It permanently reorganizes the decision environment and the enjoyment environment. The legally relevant allegation, then, can take stable forms. It may consist of informational inadequacy, when the information exists but does not guide a useful decision. It may consist of a breach of good faith, when the architecture of the environment hinders the formation of free and rational will. It may consist of objective disloyalty, when relevant changes are communicated in a ritualized, dispersed manner or at an inadequate moment. And it may consist of improper management of expectation, when offer, interface and decision flow are organized to produce an asymmetric perception of advantage, risk or equivalence. It is precisely at this level that the category leaves the abstract plane and enters the real CDC, because the transparency required by the system <1>p. 607</1> does not mean the mere formal existence of texts, but respect for the normal interests of the consumer and the organization of material conditions for a considered decision<2><3>689</3></2>.

On the second plane, operationalization requires shifting the evidence from impressionistic ground to the communicational and architectural materiality of supply. The object of proof is not the inner state of the consumer considered in isolation. What is proven is the objective form of the decision path and of the enjoyment regime as structured by the platform. This allows semiotic vulnerability to be reconstructed through external, replicable and institutionally controllable elements. The first source of support is interface trails and decision flow: dated screenshots, screen recordings, purchase, acceptance, upgrade and confirmation screens, messages about rarity, equivalence, time remaining, discount, event or change. What is relevant there is not the user's subjective memory, but the architecture actually presented. The allegation ceases to be “I did not understand” and becomes “the environment was designed this way”.

The second source of support is the history of the offer and of mutability. The advertising and institutional promise is compared with the enjoyment actually delivered and with its later changes. What one seeks to show is not generic subjective frustration, but possible relevant degradation, loss of functional equivalence or unilateral reconfiguration with material impact on the experience. In IOCs, this comparison is central because the object is not exhausted by its nominal existence. Its legal character depends on enjoyment being maintained in functionally recognizable terms. To prove a change in the environment, in the utility, in the comparability or in the intelligibility of the experience is to prove a change in the supply regime itself.

The third source of support concerns advertising and its identifying documents. Promotional pieces, posts, campaigns, influencers, disclaimers, asterisks, cascading cross-references and fine print serve to map how the expectation was produced and where the <1>p. 608</1> relevant conditions were hidden, diluted or moved to zones of low visibility. The same applies to proof of informational noise. Excess becomes opacity when there is fragmentation, circular cross-references, indecipherable technical language, internal contradictions, a gap between information and the moment of decision or displacement of the essential away from the point of choice. The evidentiary core is to demonstrate not the absence of text, but the structural inadequacy of the communication for purposes of useful understanding.

This evidentiary model also requires recognizing that semiotic asymmetry projects itself into an asymmetry of evidence. Whoever controls the service controls, to a large extent, the decisive records of the relation. <1>Logs</1>, version histories, transactions, interface parameters, change communications and relevant technical documentation tend to remain in the supplier's possession. For this reason, the operationalization of the category must be accompanied by requests for preservation and production of minimum documentation of the supply. Without this, the consumer is prevented from demonstrating precisely what the IOC regime makes central. This is not a procedural favor. It is a matter of neutralizing the private concentration of the means of reconstructing the case. The CDC's language for this response already exists. Consumer protection admits rebalancing techniques when the informational failure and the form of the bond reveal a material defect in the formation or performance of the relation<2><3>690</3></2>.

On the third plane, semiotic vulnerability must lead to foreseeable consequences. The first group is informational. If the problem is the decisional inadequacy of the communication, the request cannot simply be “more information”. The remedy is qualified information, organized in a clear, adequate and verifiable way at the moment of decision. This may mean conspicuous highlighting of the essential, reorganization of the communication flow, prohibition of obscure cross-references or the requirement of materially useful notice about relevant changes. The second group is that of control of the offer and of practices. When the legitimate expectation was produced by ambiguity, relevant omission or semiotic management of the perception of value, correction, inhibition and restoration of the frustration produced are appropriate.

<1>p. 609</1> The third group is that of the ineffectiveness of obscurity. Clauses, internal rules, cascading terms and ritual acceptances that operate as semiotic traps should not be treated as a robust manifestation of consent. When language hinders real understanding of the meaning and scope of adhesion, the consumer-law system already authorizes neutralizing the effectiveness of obscurity in the concrete case. The fourth group is evidentiary. In the face of the concentration of records, preservation and production of the trails of supply are appropriate, with a rational redistribution of the burden and presumptions favorable to the consumer when the supplier does not cooperate or keeps the evidence in a black box.

This scheme shows that semiotic vulnerability is not a decorative concept. It organizes allegation, evidence and request. What is alleged is a structural asymmetry of meaning produced by the supply regime. What is proven is the communicational and architectural materiality of that asymmetry. What is requested is the correction of the decision environment, the neutralization of obscurity, the production of records and the restoration of the affected enjoyment. The category thus ceases to be a theoretical label and comes to function as an operator. It is precisely this that prepares the passage to open auditability and to the qualification of abusive teleology as a defect of the supply regime itself. Warat helps to recall only the core of the mechanism being converted into a legal allegation: the problem lies not in an inner deficiency of the consumer, but in a structure of language and framing that unequally takes from him the power to constitute the meaning of his own relation<1><2>691</2></1>.

The operationalization of semiotic vulnerability does not start from the idea of the consumer's individual inattention, but from the recognition of an unequal distribution of legally relevant communicational competence. The problem is not to censure the user for not having read or understood everything, but to identify that contractual and operational communication was structured according to codes, references and forms of expression whose full apprehension is not equally distributed among the participants in the consumer relation. At this point, Gnerre functions as a subsidiary reinforcement in recalling that the linguistic registers of greatest prestige and power are not universally accessible. As the author observes, "only a part of the members of complex societies, for example, has access to a 'cultivated' or 'standard variety, generally considered 'the language', and typically associated with contents of prestige. The standard language is a communicative system within reach of a reduced part of the members of a community" <1>Gnerre</1><2>(Gnerre, 1991, p. 6)</2>. The same mechanism appears when the platform adjusts syntax, lexicon and frame of references so as to restrict the effective addressees of the message, since, as the author adds, "to reduce or broaden the range of the possible receivers of political and cultural messages it is enough to adjust the syntax, the frame of references and the lexicon" <3>Gnerre</3><4>(Gnerre, 1991, p. 21)</4>. In IOCs, this reinforces that semiotic vulnerability concerns the very communicational architecture of supply, and not a psychological failure or mere negligence in reading. <5>↩</5>

The operationalization of semiotic vulnerability, in the sphere of IOCs, requires bringing it back to the concrete decision plane of the CDC, that is, to the ground on which the asymmetry of meaning is converted into legally relevant informational inadequacy, breach of objective good faith and grounds for requests to correct the supply regime itself. Marques offers decisive support in stating that good faith, made concrete in the consumer relation, "means mandatory transparency toward the contractual partner, a mandatory respect for the normal interests of the other contracting party, a positive action by the stronger contractual partner to allow the weaker contractual partner the conditions necessary for the formation of a free and rational will", adding that ensuring information, protection against the pressures of sales methods and time for reflection are legal objectives of this pursuit of a rational decision by the consumer <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 812)</2>. In a convergent sense, the author argues that the possibility of prior knowledge of the contractual text and of the obligations it contains is an "essential condition for the formation of a truly free, conscious, 'rational will", which is why art. 46 allows the consumer to request in court release from the bond due to a failure of the supplier's duties of information <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 898-899)</4>. This allows semiotic vulnerability to be translated into allegation, evidence and request within the real CDC. <5>↩</5>

The CDC does not limit itself to recognizing, in theory, that the consumer's freedom of choice may be compromised by inadequate contractual and informational structures; it provides for concrete corrective consequences precisely to rebalance the decision environment when the formation of will proves materially defective. Marques formulates this reasoning by stating that, in the face of the structural "pressures" that unbalance contracting in consumer society, there arises the need for a "rebalancing legal response", exemplified by control of the content of the contract, by "a new informative formalism" and by the right of withdrawal without cause, all this "with the aim of rebalancing or supplying the 'factual failure' in the freedom or will of the weaker contracting party." <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 287)</2>. The author also highlights the case-law tendency to declare the ineffectiveness of contractual clauses and even of entire consumer bonds on the basis of arts. 46 and 54, § 4, of the CDC, precisely because of problems of form and contractual drafting revealing insufficient information and warning to the consumer <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1304)</4>. This authorizes structuring corrective requests aimed not only at later reparation, but at the refinement of the supply regime itself. <5>↩</5>

Warat offers a bridge for tracing back the mechanism underlying semiotic vulnerability. The relevant asymmetry is not founded on a psychological incapacity of the consumer, but on an unequal distribution of power through language, communicational framing and ritualization of meaning. The author warns that the function of domination should not be analyzed “from a psychologistic point of view”, since senders and receivers are institutionally situated and their discourses operate as supports of a mediatized ideology <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 67)</2>. The inequality, therefore, lies not in a supposed subjective deficiency of the addressee, but in the way the communicational structure is organized in advance to favor certain poles of definition, interpretation and legitimation. This key is reinforced when Warat shows that the producer of discourse can secure for himself “the monopoly of the constitution of the denotative field”, selecting designative properties for persuasive purposes and leaving the receivers “asleep to the discussion of the persuasively proposed designative criteria” <3>Warat</3><4>(Warat, 1984, p. 70)</4>. It is precisely this kind of communicational disciplining, and not an inner failure of the consumer, that can be traced back to the legal allegation of semiotic vulnerability in IOCs. <5>↩</5>
